name: Citation Graphs Over Time
title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time are the study of how scholarly references accumulate, connect and shift across years, rather than as a single frozen snapshot. The unit of analysis is the directed edge from one paper to another, and the interesting questions concern when that edge appeared, how quickly it was followed, and whether the citing community later abandoned or reinforced it. This sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where the goal is often to trace how an idea, method or dataset moved through a literature. A static graph answers who cites whom, while a temporal one answers when and in what order.

sections.body: Citation graphs over time are the study of how scholarly references accumulate, connect and shift across years, rather than as a single frozen snapshot. The unit of analysis is the directed edge from one paper to another, and the interesting questions concern when that edge appeared, how quickly it was followed, and whether the citing community later abandoned or reinforced it. This sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where the goal is often to trace how an idea, method or dataset moved through a literature. A static graph answers who cites whom, while a temporal one answers when and in what order.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is bibliographic metadata: titles, authors, venues, years and reference lists, usually drawn from sources such as Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or Web of Science. Storage tends to be a graph database or a columnar store, because the same edge set is queried both as a network and as a time series. Processing pipelines deduplicate author names and venue strings, resolve references to persistent identifiers like DOIs, and attach a timestamp to each edge. Visualisation layers then render the graph at a chosen time window, often with a slider or animation to show growth.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work usually begins by defining a cohort, such as papers citing a seed work within a date range, then extracting their reference lists and normalising the identifiers. From there, analysts compute time aware measures: citation half life, burst detection, co citation over sliding windows, and the changing position of a node in the network. Community detection is run per period so that clusters can be compared across years rather than assumed stable. Validation matters, because missing or misparsed references can create apparent trends that are really gaps in the source data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is central, since a temporal claim is only as good as the coverage of the underlying index for each year. Analysts should record which database supplied each edge, when it was retrieved, and how references were matched, because coverage and matching rules change over time. Licensing varies by source, and some indexes restrict bulk reuse or redistribution of reference data. Citation counts and graph position are descriptive signals, not measures of quality or impact, and they should not be used to judge individual researchers without context.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuously updated graphs that refresh as new papers appear, rather than annual snapshots. Better identifier resolution and open metadata are making it easier to link preprints, datasets and software to the papers that use them, which widens what counts as a citation. Expect more work on detecting emerging topics early and on modelling how citation behaviour itself changes, including shifts in self citation and venue prestige. The open questions are about coverage bias across languages and regions, and about how to keep temporal analyses reproducible when the underlying indexes keep moving.
